text_blocks.snippet: Type 2 diabetes develops slowly, and many people have mild or no symptoms in the early stages.
When early signs appear, they are usually subtle and include:

list.snippet: Frequent urination: Needing to go to the bathroom more often, especially at night, as your kidneys try to flush out extra sugar.
Increased thirst: Feeling unusually thirsty or dry-mouthed because frequent urination leads to mild dehydration.
Persistent fatigue: Feeling very tired or drained because your cells cannot properly absorb glucose (sugar) for energy.
Constant hunger: Feeling hungry even after eating, because your body fails to convert blood sugar into cellular fuel.
Blurred vision: High blood sugar pulling fluid from the lenses of your eyes, making it hard to focus.
Slow-healing cuts or sores: Minor bruises, cuts, or blisters taking much longer to heal due to poor circulation and high blood sugar.
Tingling or numbness: A "pins and needles" sensation or loss of feeling in your hands or feet, which is an early sign of nerve irritation (neuropathy).
Frequent infections: More frequent urinary tract infections (UTIs), yeast infections, or skin issues, since bacteria and fungi thrive on extra sugar.
Darkened skin patches (acanthosis nigricans): Velvety, dark patches of skin typically appearing around the neck, armpits, or groin, which can signal insulin resistance.

text_blocks.snippet: Because symptoms can be easy to miss, doctors rely on simple blood tests to catch the condition early or identify prediabetes:

list.snippet: Fasting plasma glucose test: Measures blood sugar after an 8-hour fast; 126 mg/dL or higher indicates diabetes.
A1C test: Shows your average blood sugar level over the past 2 to 3 months; 6.5% or higher indicates diabetes.
Random plasma glucose test: Checked at any time of day; 200 mg/dL or higher (with symptoms) indicates diabetes.
